title: Grand View Estates Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Grand View Estates wells have a 340-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, permit history, and estimated drilling costs.
h1: Grand View Estates, Colorado Well Guide
intro_html:
Grand View Estates sits in Denver Basin country, where permitted wells within about 5 miles show a median drilled depth of 340 feet. The middle half runs from 196 to 500 feet, so a nearby well is useful evidence but not a guarantee for your lot.

Records show a median reported pump yield of 14.0 gallons per minute, although yield data is available for only 1,696 wells. This page uses Colorado DWR permit records to explain what buyers and builders should ask about near Sierra Ridge, Meridian Village, Stonegate, Meridian, Stepping Stone, and Dove Valley.

sections.heading: Grand View Estates well depth: plan for variable drilling
sections.html:
Wells around Grand View Estates are commonly deeper than a typical shallow foothills well. The median depth is 340 feet, and the middle half extends from 196 to 500 feet. That spread matters when you request a drilling estimate: a bid based only on the median can miss a materially deeper hole.

The depth mix shows 45% of recorded wells between 300 and 600 feet, while 14% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 2,681 feet. Most permits identify Denver Basin aquifers, including Lower Dawson and Denver, while many others identify unnamed fractured bedrock. Local geology, the target aquifer, and the exact lot can change the required depth.

sections.heading: Expected well yield near Sierra Ridge and Meridian Village
sections.html:
Reported production is generally strong in this record set. The median pump yield is 14.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 12.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Among wells reporting yield, 57% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 42% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No recorded wells in this dataset fall below 1 gallon per minute, but that does not make a low-yield result impossible on an untested parcel. A well's pumping rate is not the same as storage in the well or the legal right to use water. Confirm the permit's allowed uses, test the well, and ask for a sustained production test before relying on the neighboring statistics.

sections.heading: What the water-level records show in Grand View Estates
sections.html:
The reported median static water level is 250 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 98 to 410 feet. That is a measurement of depth to water when the well is not being pumped, not the total drilling depth. A builder needs both figures when planning pump setting, electrical work, pressure equipment, and a reliable water supply.

The decade series does not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 132 feet in the 1970s, 260 feet in the 1980s, 685 feet in the 2000s, 332 feet in the 2010s, and 182 feet in the 2020s. Only 196 wells report static water level, so treat this as historical context rather than a prediction for your lot.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Stonegate and Meridian
sections.html:
Colorado DWR permit records show long-term drilling activity in the area, with the largest decade totals in the 1970s and 1980s. Permits issued by decade were 1,073 in the 1970s, 998 in the 1980s, 782 in the 1990s, 629 in the 2000s, 448 in the 2010s, and 263 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most frequent driller names are Hier Drilling Co Inc, associated with Bruce A. Hier, with 847 records; Hier Drilling Co., associated with Peter J. Hier, with 597; and Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 485. These counts describe permit records, not current availability or a recommendation. Verify licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new well may cost in Grand View Estates
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 340-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to about $17,000 to $23,800. That is not the completed water system.

Adding the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical brings the modeled finished-well range to about $23,000 to $35,800. A deeper-than-median hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, power distance, or site excavation can change the bid. Ask the contractor what footage is included, how extra depth is priced, and which equipment and connection work are excluded.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. Confirm the well's permitted use, production test, water quality, casing, grout, pump condition, and measured static level. Household-use wells are commonly exempt wells, but the permit still controls allowed use. Pumping limits and water-right requirements can matter, especially in an over-appropriated basin where an augmentation plan may be needed for additional use.

Environmental records within about 10 miles include 113 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a specific parcel. Order an appropriate water test and review the location of septic systems, drainfields, wells, and proposed structures before closing or excavating.

sections.heading: A practical lot checklist for Dove Valley-area buyers
sections.html:
Start with the nearest permitted wells, not a countywide average. Compare wells in Grand View Estates and nearby Sierra Ridge, Meridian Village, Stonegate, Meridian, Stepping Stone, and Dove Valley for depth, aquifer name, yield, and water level. Then have a Colorado well contractor inspect the records and identify what remains unknown.

Before purchase, verify the permit and use restrictions with DWR, obtain the well construction and pump documents, and make the sale contingent on water-quality and production testing when appropriate. For a new build, confirm access for a drill rig, septic setbacks, electrical routing, storage needs, and the legal water supply before finalizing the house site. A promising neighboring well lowers uncertainty; it does not remove parcel-specific drilling risk.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Grand View Estates?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within about 5 miles of Grand View Estates is 340 feet. The middle half runs from 196 to 500 feet, and 45% of recorded wells are between 300 and 600 feet. Some wells exceed 600 feet, so use nearby records for planning rather than treating the median as a guarantee.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Grand View Estates?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 340-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $17,000 to $23,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $23,000 to $35,800. Access, extra depth, casing, grout, and power distance can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Grand View Estates?
faq.a: Reported pump yield has a median of 14.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Among the 1,696 wells reporting yield, 57% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 42% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Test the individual well before relying on it.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Grand View Estates?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit record alone. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 113 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features, and 8 EPA cleanup sites. These records do not establish contamination at your parcel. Have the well tested for contaminants appropriate to the property and review its construction and septic history.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Grand View Estates?
faq.a: The available series does not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 132 feet in the 1970s, 260 feet in the 1980s, 685 feet in the 2000s, 332 feet in the 2010s, and 182 feet in the 2020s. Only 196 wells report static levels, so these figures are historical context, not a parcel-specific forecast.
